report.source_text: While in the surgical ICU, the patient developed worsening acute allograft dysfunction, over her CKD with hyperkalaemia and oliguria. General nephrology and transplant nephrology services were consulted. Acute allograft dysfunction was thought to be secondary to acute tubular necrosis due to the massive retroperitoneal bleed, hypotension and possibly a component of contrast nephropathy. A renal ultrasound of the patient’s transplanted kidney demonstrated normal flow during her hospitalisation. Due to a potassium of 7.7 mmol/L, haemodialysis was initiated via temporary internal jugular venous trialysis catheter. She underwent three consecutive days of haemodialysis. Her creatinine peaked at 4.18 mg/dL, with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 13 mL/min. Fortunately, her kidney function and urine output improved and she did not need any further dialysis.

Two units of uncrossmatched O+packed red blood cells were given due to presumed intra-abdominal bleeding causing haemorrhagic shock.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A woman in her 30s with a history of kidney transplant and IgA nephropathy presented to the emergency department with progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain radiating to her left flank, accompanied by signs of hypovolemic shock including diaphoresis, pallor, cool skin, diminished capillary refill, and hypotension. Initial laboratory findings revealed significant anemia (hemoglobin 82 g/L, decreased from baseline 123 g/L) and elevated lactate (2.6). A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrated large volume hemoperitoneum and a left retroperitoneal hematoma with contrast extravasation from the left renal artery. The CT scan identified a ruptured AML in the region of the patient’s atrophic native left kidney as the suspected cause of hemorrhage. Initial resuscitation included crystalloid infusion and two units of packed red blood cells. The hemorrhage was definitively managed by successful embolization of the patient’s left renal artery with ethanol and coils. Following the intervention, the patient developed acute allograft dysfunction with hyperkalemia and oliguria, requiring temporary hemodialysis, which subsequently improved.
